paras: The killing of Melvin Fair took place in early February 1903 near Luverne, Crenshaw County, Alabama, when constable James Stallings and John Lawson shot a Black man they had come to arrest for leaving a labor contract. The two men said he had fired on them first, but a grand jury indicted both for first-degree murder in March and a judge refused them bail.

According to the accused, the man was bound by a labor contract with Amos Sanders of Beat 9 and had left him. Stallings and Lawson carried a warrant for his arrest approved by Justice Tate of Crenshaw County, and a later report described the charge as a "violation of a civil contract."

The two men went to the man's home on the Bimbo place, about five miles below Luverne. In their account, he fired at them three times when they tried to arrest him, and they returned fire and killed him instantly. No other version of the shooting appears in the coverage.

On the evening of February 5, Charlie May, a Crenshaw County deputy sheriff, brought Stallings and Lawson to Troy and turned them over to Sheriff Reeves, because there was smallpox in the Luverne jail. A preliminary hearing was set before Justice Brooks of Luverne for that Saturday, but no report of it was found.

At the March term of court, the grand jury under foreman J. F. Reynolds indicted Lawson and Stallings for murder in the first degree. At a habeas corpus hearing, Judge J. C. Richardson heard the defendants' evidence and sent them to jail without bail, with C. R. Bricken prosecuting as solicitor. No report of a trial or its outcome was found.

The only coverage found was two specials in the Montgomery Advertiser, and no Black-press report was found. The Troy dispatch ran under the headline "ACCUSED OF KILLING NEGRO" with the subhead "A Constable and Another White Man Under Arrest," and it gave the accused men's version of the shooting without comment. The Luverne report, headed "HELD WITHOUT BAIL," covered the March court session and described the accused as "two prominent citizens of Pike County" and the victim as "Melvin Long, a Negro." Neither report commented on the killing or on the labor-contract arrest behind it.

The two reports give the victim's surname differently: the Troy dispatch called him Melvin Fair, while the Luverne report called him Melvin Long. They also differ on Lawson's status, with the first describing him only as "another white man" and the second calling both men constables of Pike County.

reader.title: Killing of Melvin Fair
bases: A constable and a companion (both called constables in A2) killed a Black man while serving a warrant for his arrest for leaving a labor contract; no crowd was involved (A1, A2).

Two separate specials to the Montgomery Advertiser, from Troy (A1) and from Luverne (A2), agree that Stallings and Lawson killed a Black man near Luverne while trying to arrest him for breaking a labor contract, though they give his surname differently.

framing.detail: The Troy special ran under 'ACCUSED OF KILLING NEGRO. A Constable and Another White Man Under Arrest' and gave the accused men's version without comment.
